origin_units: crates/idboardd/src/main.rs#serve named-pipe connection and one JSON frame::crates/idboardd/src/main.rs#accept loop worker pool and Board mutex::ATTACK-CLASSES.md#Business logic
title: The single global Board mutex is acquired before the peer-controlled read and write, so one stalled unauthenticated pipe connection blocks every identity
description: Principal 1 is any unauthenticated local process. It performs a single CreateFile on \\.\pipe\idboardd-<USERNAME>, sends no bytes at all (or, on the write variant, any well-formed line and then stops reading), and holds the connection open. The worker that picks it up has already called board.lock() at main.rs:135 on the one and only Arc<Mutex<Board>> at main.rs:117, and that guard is passed into serve(&mut guard, stream) at main.rs:139 and held for the whole call. serve's first act is the unbounded read at main.rs:177 and its last is the unbounded write at main.rs:194, both of which are peer-paced because apply_timeouts installs no deadline on the primary platform (ipc/lib.rs:183-194). The remaining three workers each pull a stream at main.rs:130 and then block on the same mutex at main.rs:135, so the four worker slots are consumed; the accept loop keeps filling the bounded channel at main.rs:148 until 64 are pending, at which point the accept loop itself blocks and the daemon accepts nobody. No legitimate identity is served for the duration. This is not self-harm: a DIFFERENT identity's signed post, read or handshake is the traffic that is stopped, and it is stopped because the board is a single serialised shared resource (main.rs:114-117). The documented risk model at main.rs:21-24 and README.md:326-329 describes only per-worker throughput loss and materially understates this. Attacker cost is one connect and zero crafted bytes; the effect is durable until the attacker closes, requires no privilege and no key, and is not rate-limited by anything in the tree. Smallest fix: in the worker loop, perform idboard_ipc::split and idboard_ipc::read_frame before acquiring the board lock, and take the lock only around board.handle(&req); move the rejection eprintln! out of the critical section as well. Board::handle performs only bounded local crypto and SQLite work (idboardd/src/lib.rs:87-125), so this change removes all peer-paced blocking from the critical section without changing any security decision.
claimed_root_cause: The worker loop acquires the process-wide Mutex<Board> at crates/idboardd/src/main.rs:135 before performing the peer-paced blocking read at crates/idboardd/src/main.rs:177 and blocking write at crates/idboardd/src/main.rs:194, so the single shared serialisation point covers the whole untrusted request/response exchange rather than only the bounded board mutation.

trace.description: idboard_ipc::accept(&listener) returns a Stream for any local process that connects to the named pipe. accept then calls apply_timeouts, which is a no-op on this platform (ipc/lib.rs:189).

trace.scope: accept loop, main thread
trace.description: tx.send(s) hands the stream to the bounded sync_channel built at main.rs:111 with QUEUE_DEPTH=64. This is the only queue bound; tx.send blocks when it is full.

trace.scope: worker thread, one of WORKERS=4 from main.rs:25
trace.description: board.lock() is taken on the single Arc<Mutex<Board>> created at main.rs:117, before any byte has been read from the peer. The PoisonError arm at main.rs:137 recovers via into_inner, so this is the normal path.

trace.scope: worker thread
trace.description: serve(&mut guard, stream) is called with the guard still alive, so the global board lock is held for the entire duration of serve (main.rs:168-197). The other three workers now block on the same mutex at main.rs:135 as each takes its own stream.

trace.scope: attacker-paced blocking read inside the critical section
trace.description: idboard_ipc::read_frame blocks in BufRead::fill_buf at ipc/lib.rs:210 until a newline, EOF, or error. With no deadline installed, a peer that sends nothing holds the global board mutex indefinitely.

trace.scope: attacker-paced blocking write inside the critical section
trace.description: Second, independent trigger. main.rs:191 produces a DaemonResponse even for an unparseable frame, so a peer needs no key and no valid signature: send any well-formed line, then never read. write_frame blocks in write_all at ipc/lib.rs:262 with no send deadline (ipc/lib.rs:189), holding the same global mutex.

evidence.description: let board = std::sync::Arc::new(std::sync::Mutex::new(board)); -- the single process-wide serialisation point shared by all identities and all workers.
let mut guard = match board.lock() { ... } -- lock taken before the peer read; this is the defect location and the smallest-fix location.
serve(&mut guard, stream); -- the guard is passed by mutable borrow, so it lives for the whole of serve, which contains the read at :177, the stderr write at :183 and the socket write at :194.

let (tx, rx) = sync_channel::<idboard_ipc::Stream>(QUEUE_DEPTH); -- the bounded queue; saturation occurs when the remaining workers are blocked on the board mutex, so 64 queued connections stop the accept loop at :148.
const WORKERS: usize = 4; -- combined with the single board mutex, all four slots are consumed by one attacker plus three legitimate requests that then queue behind the lock.

Doc comment asserting the consequence is 'a client that connects and then stalls occupies a worker until it disconnects ... this costs throughput'. The documented model omits the single Arc<Mutex<Board>> taken at :135, which converts a four-connection throughput issue into a one-connection cross-identity outage.
Err(e) => DaemonResponse::err(...) -- establishes that the write-side trigger needs no valid frame content and therefore no key.
eprintln!("idboardd: {}", rejection_line(...)) -- a third blocking-capable operation inside the critical section; a stalled or full stderr sink also freezes the shared board.

pub fn handle(&mut self, req: &DaemonRequest) -> DaemonResponse -- bounded local work only (verify_with_key at :116, store.append at :188, store.read at :209, store.touch at :205/:230, store.last_seq at :229), so taking the lock after read_frame is sufficient and does not weaken any security decision.

'No I/O timeouts on Windows named pipes ... a client that connects and then stalls costs throughput rather than the process.' Documents the missing deadline but not its interaction with the single board mutex, so the accepted-risk statement is inaccurate for the multi-identity case.

blockers: no OS-enforced sandbox available on the audit host to execute the bounded local check

validation_plan.local: On an isolated Windows machine, build the workspace, set IDBOARD_HOME to a fresh temp directory containing a two-identity config.toml (identity.a and identity.b, each with a generated pubkey, one channel with post=["*"] read=["*"]) and a fresh idboard.db. Start idboardd in the background. Phase 1 (read trigger): open a handle to the daemon pipe with a minimal client that connects and then writes ZERO bytes and stays open, using a 5-second sleep before any cleanup. While it is open, from a second process run `idboard post --identity b --channel general --body still-alive` (the wrapper signs and hits the daemon pipe) with a 30-second timeout. Expected observation to confirm the finding: the phase-1 connection remains open, the phase-2 wrapper times out with no DaemonResponse, and idboardd still shows 4 workers ready with no accept progress. Phase 2 (write trigger, no key needed): repeat, but have the stalled client write one syntactically valid JSON line and then never read the reply. Same expected observation. Control: close the stalled handle, then re-run phase 2 and confirm the wrapper succeeds, proving the daemon recovers only when the attacker disconnects. Stop at the first confirmed timeout; do not increase the number of concurrent stalled handles.
validation_plan.deployment: None. This is a single-host local daemon with no autoscaling, no upstream gateway and no per-tenant quota; the shared resource is the in-process Arc<Mutex<Board>>, so nothing outside the repository can bound it.

origin_units: crates/idboardd/src/main.rs#serve named-pipe connection and one JSON frame::crates/idboard-ipc/src/lib.rs#apply_timeouts platform I/O deadline support::ATTACK-CLASSES.md#Business logic
title: apply_timeouts swallows ErrorKind::Unsupported, so no socket in the tree carries an I/O deadline on the primary platform and read_frame_from has no independent termination condition
description: The invariant is that every read of peer-controlled bytes terminates. Source establishes the opposite. apply_timeouts at ipc/lib.rs:181-194 calls set_recv_timeout and set_send_timeout (ipc/lib.rs:183-184) and discards ErrorKind::Unsupported at ipc/lib.rs:189, then returns Ok(()) at ipc/lib.rs:193. On Windows named pipes, which the doc at ipc/lib.rs:170-180 states is the normal case and is the only platform the e2e harness exercises (crates/idboard/tests/e2e.rs:41 hardcodes a .exe suffix), Ok(()) means no deadline was installed. read_frame_from at ipc/lib.rs:206-241 then has no time-based exit at all: it loops on fill_buf at ipc/lib.rs:210 and exits only on a newline (ipc/lib.rs:222), a clean EOF (ipc/lib.rs:215), or an error. The sole bound on peer bytes is MAX_FRAME_BYTES at ipc/lib.rs:233-235, which is conditional on bytes arriving and therefore never trips for a peer that sends none or sends a partial line. The same swallow removes the send deadline, so write_all at ipc/lib.rs:262 is likewise unbounded. Both are accepted risks in the documentation, but the documented impact -- 'costs throughput rather than the process' (README.md:326-329, main.rs:21-24) -- understates the consequence because of the separate lock-acquisition ordering defect in idboardd/src/main.rs:135, which turns a per-worker retention into a global one. The two defects compound: fixing only this one still serialises the whole board behind up to IO_TIMEOUT per stalled peer, and fixing only the lock ordering still lets four stalled connections plus a 64-deep queue halt the accept loop. The test applying_timeouts_never_fails_on_either_platform at ipc/lib.rs:423-432 asserts only that apply_timeouts returns Ok, so the suite pins the swallow rather than any deadline, and no test anywhere releases a stalled reader after IO_TIMEOUT.
claimed_root_cause: crates/idboard-ipc/src/lib.rs:189 discards ErrorKind::Unsupported from set_recv_timeout/set_send_timeout and reports success, so on the primary platform IO_TIMEOUT is never installed and read_frame_from (crates/idboard-ipc/src/lib.rs:206-241) retains no independent termination condition beyond peer-supplied bytes.

MAX_FRAME_BYTES at ipc/lib.rs:233-235 bounds accumulated bytes only once bytes arrive, so a connection that sends nothing or a partial line never terminates the read.

evidence.description: Err(ref e) if e.kind() == std::io::ErrorKind::Unsupported => {} -- the swallow. This is the root-cause line for this candidate.
pub const IO_TIMEOUT: std::time::Duration = std::time::Duration::from_secs(10); -- the intended deadline, which becomes dead configuration on the primary platform.

Doc comment: '**Windows named pipes do not support these.** ... Failing there would make the daemon unusable on its primary target platform, so we proceed without a deadline instead.' Confirms the behaviour is deliberate and platform-wide, not an incidental error.
if buf.len() + n > MAX_FRAME_BYTES { return Err(IpcError::FrameTooLarge); } -- the only bound in read_frame_from, and it is conditional on bytes arriving, so it does not bound a stalled reader.

fn applying_timeouts_never_fails_on_either_platform() -- asserts only that apply_timeouts returns Ok, and its comment at :421-422 states the Unsupported path must be tolerated. No test asserts that a stalled reader is released after IO_TIMEOUT on any platform, so the suite pins the swallow rather than a deadline.

The unbounded read is consumed here inside the board-lock critical section, which is what escalates this root cause from per-worker retention to the cross-identity outage reported under idboardd.serve.board_mutex_held_across_peer_blocking_io.
The unbounded write is consumed here, also inside the critical section, and is reachable with no key because main.rs:191 always produces a response.

'The daemon runs a fixed worker pool, so a client that connects and then stalls costs throughput rather than the process.' The accepted-risk statement is accurate only for the worker slots, not for the single Mutex<Board> taken at main.rs:135.

validation_plan.local: On an isolated Windows machine, confirm the two source facts with a bounded fixture and no stress or saturation. Fact 1, the deadline is not installed: bind a listener with idboard_ipc::bind, connect one client, accept it, and assert that a single read_frame that the client never feeds is not released -- measured elapsed time must exceed IO_TIMEOUT (10 s) with a hard 60 s cap, then close the handle. Fact 2, the compounding with the daemon: with idboardd running under a fresh IDBOARD_HOME, open one pipe handle, write zero bytes, and separately (second run) write one valid JSON line then stop reading; in each run, within 30 s, confirm that a second, correctly signed identity's `idboard post` receives no response. Regression case for the fix: assert that a reader that never sends a newline is released within IO_TIMEOUT, i.e. read_frame returns IpcError::Io(TimedOut) or UnexpectedEof rather than blocking past 10 s, and that a stalled writer is released symmetrically. Stop after the first confirmed observation.
validation_plan.deployment: None required to establish the source facts. The only deployment question an owner may need to answer is which platform the daemon actually runs on, since on Unix the SO_RCVTIMEO path at ipc/lib.rs:183 would apply and this candidate would not manifest; the e2e harness at crates/idboard/tests/e2e.rs:41 hardcodes a .exe suffix, so the tested platform is Windows.

origin_units: crates/idboard-core/src/wire.rs#DaemonRequest and RelayRequest JSON wire shapes::crates/idboard-ipc/src/lib.rs#read_frame newline-delimited JSON framing::ATTACK-CLASSES.md#Injection
title: Unbounded Envelope string fields admitted at the framing boundary are rendered unescaped into the daemon rejection log by an unauthenticated peer
description: Lower-trust principal: any local process on the machine, unauthenticated, able to open \\.\pipe\idboardd-<USERNAME>. Accepted value: one newline-delimited JSON frame of at most MAX_FRAME_BYTES whose envelope.sender_id and envelope.channel are arbitrary UTF-8, including CR, LF and ANSI CSI sequences. Control that should reject it: ids.rs defines validate_identity and validate_channel precisely for this, but they are wired only into Envelope::validate (crates/idboard-core/src/envelope.rs:258), which runs inside verify_with_key -- after the version branch (crates/idboardd/src/lib.rs:95) and the registration branch (:105). Neither of those two branches performs any crypto, and both produce a not-ok DaemonResponse, so the raw, unbounded strings reach rejection_line regardless of validation. Source path after that decision: crates/idboardd/src/main.rs:180-186 calls rejection_line(&req.envelope, ...) on every not-ok response, and rejection_line (crates/idboardd/src/lib.rs:242-252) interpolates env.sender_id and env.channel with Display {} at lines 246-247, then main.rs:183 writes it to the operator's stderr. Because Display does not escape, an embedded CR/LF becomes a real line break, so a single 1-frame request can emit several lines shaped exactly like genuine rejections -- for example a forged `rejected op=post claimed_sender=lead channel=deploy-approvals seq=1 code=ok detail=...` -- and terminal escape sequences in the same fields can repaint the operator's console. Stop point: the daemon's rejection log, which README and AGENTS.md name as the post-incident attribution record; no board state, key or message body is affected. Smallest fix: in rejection_line, bound and escape the interpolated fields -- truncate sender_id and channel to a fixed prefix and replace any control character with '?', or format them with {:?} as the UnknownIdentity detail already does at crates/idboardd/src/lib.rs:107-113. The defense-in-depth complement is to apply validate_identity/validate_channel to envelope.sender_id and envelope.channel at decode time in decode_frame (crates/idboard-ipc/src/lib.rs:243) so no unbounded string exists before any dispatch branch runs; note this would make a malformed-name frame decode as a structural error rather than unknown_identity, so the specific ErrorCode assertions in the e2e suite would need updating deliberately.
claimed_root_cause: The framing/decode boundary imposes no per-field length or charset bound on Envelope's string fields, and the one consumer that renders a rejected envelope on a pre-authentication path formats those fields with Display instead of an escaping formatter.

trace.scope: daemon named pipe, principal 1 (any local process, unauthenticated)

Envelope.sender_id (crates/idboard-core/src/envelope.rs:119) and Envelope.channel (envelope.rs:125) are bare String fields with no declared maximum, so both may carry up to ~1 MiB of attacker-chosen UTF-8, including 0x0D 0x0A and ESC, inside one frame.

trace.description: rejection_line interpolates env.sender_id and env.channel with Display {} (lines 246-247), which performs no escaping of CR, LF or ESC, so one request can forge additional log lines in the exact shape the operator relies on for attribution, or emit terminal control sequences.

evidence.description: The only size control before decode is the whole-frame check `if buf.len() + i > MAX_FRAME_BYTES`. MAX_FRAME_BYTES is 1 MiB (line 39); nothing narrows it per field.
`pub sender_id: String` with no serde length attribute and no declaration-level bound. Line 125 is the same for `pub channel: String`.

validate_identity rejects control characters and anything over 64 bytes, and validate_channel at line 73 does the same for 128 bytes. Both exist but run only inside Envelope::validate (envelope.rs:258), which is reached solely through verify_with_key.
The UnknownIdentity branch formats sender_id with {:?} (lines 107-113), so the detail itself is escaped; the unescaped copies are the two fields rejection_line adds at lines 246-247.
`env.sender_id,` inside a `{}`-format, and line 247 `env.channel.as_str(),` inside another `{}`. Display on a Rust str does not escape control characters.
`eprintln!("idboardd: {}", rejection_line(&req.envelope, ...))` runs for every !res.ok response, so both pre-authentication rejection branches reach the sink.

validation_plan.local: On an isolated Windows host with a scratch IDBOARD_HOME: cargo build --workspace, then run `idboardd --config <tmp>/config.toml --socket \\.\pipe\idboard-audit-<rand> --db <tmp>/board.db` with stderr redirected to <tmp>/daemon.err. From a separate unprivileged process open the pipe and write exactly one line (no embedded raw newline in the JSON structure, terminated by a single \n, total under 1 MiB) whose envelope.sender_id contains a JSON-escaped \r\n followed by a forged rejection-shaped line. Expectation: the daemon replies with ok=false and error=bad_request (the version branch), and <tmp>/daemon.err grows by two or more lines rather than one, the second of which matches ^rejected op= and carries the injected claimed_sender=. Repeat with v=1 and an unregistered sender_id to exercise the :105 branch, and repeat ten times to assert the line count grows by at least 20 for ten requests. Control: the same ten requests with a single-character sender_id must grow the file by exactly ten lines.
validation_plan.deployment: On a host where the pipe ACL question matters, have the operator read the security descriptor of \\.\pipe\idboardd-<USERNAME> (Get-Acl on the pipe, or an equivalent handle listing) and record who may open it for read/write. If only the creating user and SYSTEM are granted, the affected principal is same-user and the finding is audit-trail integrity for the operator; if a broader group is granted, it extends to cross-account log forgery. Neither fact is visible in this repository.

origin_units: crates/idboard-acl/src/lib.rs#Config::load config.toml::crates/idboard-acl/src/lib.rs#Config::from_toml pubkey registration no trust on first use::ATTACK-CLASSES.md#Cryptography and secrets
title: config.toml is the sole trust root for the identity-to-key map and is consumed by a bare read with no ownership or permission check, while the only confinement helper in the tree is Unix-only
description: The entire no-trust-on-first-use guarantee is implemented in from_toml: a key enters the registry only because the operator wrote it into config.toml, and the daemon then verifies every message against that key. Config::load performs that step as an unconditional std::fs::read_to_string of whatever bytes are at an environment- or flag-derived path. It never checks the file's owner, never checks its permissions or DACL, never rejects a symlink or reparse point, and never verifies an integrity digest. The state root is created by Store::open through layout::ensure_dir, the unrestricted create_dir_all, rather than ensure_private_dir; and ensure_private_dir, the only helper that would restrict the directory, sets a mode solely under #[cfg(unix)] and compiles to a no-op on Windows, which is the project's primary target. So on Windows the entire custody of the file that decides who may be `lead` reduces to inherited NTFS ACLs that no code in the tree sets and no code in the tree verifies; layout.rs:163-166 states the assumption in a comment and calls it adequate, but the assumption is never enforced. A repo-wide grep for acl, dacl, security_descriptor, set_permissions, from_mode and permissions across the workspace returns no Windows file ACL and no named-pipe security-descriptor code at all. If the effective DACL permits any principal other than the owning account to write that file, that principal registers a key of its own for any existing identity name and is immediately authorised on every channel that name may use, while the real agent is locked out with the loud rotation warning as the only signal. Whether that DACL permits it is a platform fact outside the source, so this is reported as needing validation rather than confirmed.
claimed_root_cause: The trust-root file is loaded by a single unconditional read that performs no custody check, and the one directory-confinement helper in the codebase is compiled out on the primary platform, so custody of the registry that decides every identity's signing key is asserted by a source comment rather than established by code.

trace.scope: Config::load, invoked by idboardd/src/main.rs:71 with the path from args.config or layout::config_path (idboardd/src/main.rs:67)
trace.description: The daemon's identity registry is loaded from a path that an environment variable (IDBOARD_CONFIG) or a command-line flag selects, with no custody precondition on the file.

trace.scope: Config::load body
trace.description: std::fs::read_to_string(path) with no ownership, permission, DACL, symlink or integrity check of any kind, and no canonicalisation. Whatever bytes are present become the trust root.

trace.scope: from_toml identity loop, identities.insert
trace.description: The parsed key becomes Identity.public_key, and the fingerprint is derived from it at :207 rather than read from config, so a substituted key is fully self-consistent and invisible to the fingerprint cross-check at keys.rs:308-317. Presence and parse failures at :169-191 are fatal, but they only constrain the file's syntax, never its provenance.

trace.scope: Board::dispatch, identity.public_key passed to verify_with_key after the registry lookup at :105
trace.description: The key read from that file is the sole authority for the identity. Whoever controls the file's bytes controls which key that name maps to, and therefore full read and post authority on every channel the name may use, plus the ability to deny the genuine agent.

evidence.description: std::fs::read_to_string(path) is the complete load step; there is no ownership, permission, DACL, symlink or integrity check between the filesystem and the registry.

identities.insert publishes the parsed key as Identity.public_key, the value later used as the only verifying key; fingerprint is derived at :207 so a substituted key cannot be detected by fingerprint mismatch.

The #[cfg(not(unix))] arm of ensure_private_dir is an empty block, so on the project's primary target the function is create_dir_all and nothing else; the 0o700 mode at :172 never compiles on Windows.

The source asserts the deployment fact this candidate turns on -- that NTFS inherits ACLs from %USERPROFILE% which already grant the creating user and SYSTEM and deny Everyone, and that this is adequate -- as a comment, with no code anywhere in the tree that sets or verifies it.

Store::open creates the state root with layout::ensure_dir, the unrestricted create_dir_all, not ensure_private_dir, so the directory holding config.toml and idboard.db is never given an explicit restrictive mode or DACL by this code.

config.identity(&env.sender_id) followed by verify_with_key(&identity.public_key, env) at :116 is the entire authority decision; it trusts the loaded file completely and has no second source against which to cross-check the key.

The effective DACL of the idboard state root and of config.toml on the target platform is not source-visible. layout.rs:174-177 compiles the only confinement helper out on Windows and no code path sets or verifies a file ACL or a named-pipe security descriptor, so whether a second OS account can create or modify %USERPROFILE%\.idboard\config.toml cannot be determined from source.

validation_plan.local: On a throwaway Windows VM with two local accounts, as the owner, create %USERPROFILE%\.idboard and a minimal config.toml with one [identity.probe] whose pubkey comes from `idboard keygen probe` run on the second account, then as the second account attempt to append a second [identity.probe] entry with its own pubkey (and separately to delete-and-replace the file). Record whether the write succeeds, then start idboardd and read the startup summary to see whether both pubkeys or the substituted one took effect. Stop after the read of the summary; do not exercise the substituted identity against a live board.
validation_plan.deployment: On the host, run `icacls "%USERPROFILE%\.idboard"` and `icacls "%USERPROFILE%\.idboard\config.toml"` and record the owner, the inheritance source, and every principal granted write or modify. Compare that against the principal list this code intends, which is the single owning account plus SYSTEM. If any other principal holds write, the candidate resolves in favour of the finding; if not, the finding is closed as an inherited-ACL assumption that holds for this deployment and the residual is hardening only.

origin_units: crates/idboard-store/src/lib.rs#Store::open idboard.db::crates/idboard-store/src/lib.rs#Store::read channel scoping cursor paging and row_to_message::ATTACK-CLASSES.md#Chained vulnerabilities and trust boundaries
title: The read projection drops the signed channel field, so a StoredMessage read back from the board is not the envelope that was authenticated and cannot be re-verified
description: Starting capability: any identity the config authorises to read a channel, i.e. a child agent holding its wrapper's relay token, or any local process holding that identity's key. Accepted action: read on a channel the caller is legitimately allowed to read. State transition: none on the write side; the read side projects stored rows into a StoredMessage and hands it to the caller. The strongest source-visible control that should bind the disclosed value to the authenticated one is the ed25519 signature over Envelope::to_canonical_bytes, which covers channel; the control that is actually applied on the read side is only a channel equality predicate in the WHERE clause, which selects rows but does not carry the channel into the reconstructed value. Store::read selects `cursor, sender_id, sender_fp, seq, provenance, body, ts_ms, lower(hex(signature))` and omits channel even though channel is both the predicate and a persisted column written from the authenticated envelope on insert. row_to_message then hardcodes channel: String::new(), so the envelope a reader receives is not the envelope that was verified. Because channel is one of the nine fields covered by the signature, verify_with_key on a read-back StoredMessage must fail: the reconstructed canonical bytes differ from the bytes that authenticated the original post. The store's own comment at :271-274 justifies lower(hex(signature)) on the premise that a read-back signature stays usable for re-verification against stored data, and that premise is false for as long as the channel is dropped. Containment that was established and is not overstated: no cross-channel disclosure occurs. title: Store::open creates the idboard state root with the permissive directory helper, while the keystore directory in the same root uses the owner-only helper
description: Starting principal: a local account other than the one running the daemon, on a host where the state root is created by this code rather than pre-created by the operator. Starting capability: read access to the state directory. Accepted action: none from a peer; the relevant event is directory and file creation at daemon startup. The protected resource is idboard.db, whose tables (crates/idboard-store/src/lib.rs:78-103) hold every message body, every sender identity name, every role, every key fingerprint and public key, and the per-identity replay counter. The control that the rest of the tree relies on is owner-only creation of the state root: ensure_private_dir applies mode 0o700 under #[cfg(unix)] and the crate documentation states the rationale at crates/idboard-core/src/layout.rs:161-166. Store::open does not use it. At crates/idboard-store/src/lib.rs:114-116 it calls idboard_core::layout::ensure_dir(parent), which is a bare std::fs::create_dir_all, and then opens the database at :118 inside that directory. Two sibling call sites in the same state root take the stricter path: crates/idboard/src/keystore.rs:112 for ~/.idboard/keys, and crates/idboard/src/wrapper.rs:227 for ~/.idboard/run (which creates ~/.idboard itself as a side effect of create_dir_all and then restricts only run/). So the protection is applied per-subdirectory and never to the root, and the file carrying the message bodies is the one that gets the permissive treatment. The WAL pragma at :131 places idboard.db-wal and idboard.db-shm in the same directory as well. No numeric mode or OS ACL behaviour is asserted here: the mode create_dir_all produces is the platform default filtered by umask, and the mode SQLite uses for a newly created database file is a rusqlite/SQLite default, neither of which is visible in this repository's source. What the source does establish is the divergence itself, and that it is the mechanism the crate's own documentation names as the confidentiality control. Note that this is not the documented same-user keystore non-goal: a different local account is a different principal, and the divergence is what would let it read the board without ever touching ~/.idboard/keys.
claimed_root_cause: Store::open calls layout::ensure_dir (bare create_dir_all, platform default mode filtered by umask) for the parent of idboard.db, while Keystore::save_seed and wrapper::run_child call layout::ensure_private_dir (which additionally applies 0o700 on unix) for the subdirectories of the same state root, so no code path ever restricts the directory that holds the database and its WAL sidecars.

evidence.description: pub fn ensure_dir(dir: &Path) is exactly std::fs::create_dir_all(dir). No permission is set, on any platform.

ensure_private_dir is ensure_dir plus set_permissions(0o700) under #[cfg(unix)] (:170-173) and a no-op on Windows (:174-177). Its doc comment at :161-166 states the intent: owner-only, because NTFS inheritance from %USERPROFILE% is relied on for Windows.

The keystore directory, a sibling of the database inside the same state root, does call layout::ensure_private_dir. The divergence is therefore between two call sites in one root, not between two crates with different policies.
ensure_private_dir(&layout::run_dir()) creates ~/.idboard by way of create_dir_all and then restricts only run/, leaving the parent at the permissive default. A third call site, same divergence.

pragma_update(None, "journal_mode", "WAL") means the sensitive content is additionally present in idboard.db-wal and idboard.db-shm in the same directory, so restricting only the main file would not have been sufficient.

The messages table (:78-88) stores body and channel text; the identities table (:96-103) stores name, role, pubkey, fingerprint, last_seq and last_seen_ms. These are the resources the divergence would expose.

Store::open is the only production constructor; open_in_memory (:123) is test-only. There is no other place in the tree that creates or restricts the state root, so this single call site is the whole of the control.

title: Message body reaches the operator's terminal unescaped, so one identity can forge the rendered sender and cursor of another and drive terminal control sequences
description: Lower-trust principal: any identity the config lets post to a channel the victim reads. Starting capability: nothing beyond a legitimate `idboard post <channel> <body>` through its own wrapper, i.e. exactly the authority the design grants. Accepted value: the message body, whose only content control anywhere in the tree is a byte-length cap of 64 KiB (crates/idboard-core/src/ids.rs:92-100); no charset, control-character, or line-separator filter exists on the write path, on the relay, or on the render. The control that should reject or encode it is absent: render_message interpolates the body into a single stdout line with no escaping (crates/idboard/src/cli.rs:304-311) and the result is emitted by println! at crates/idboard/src/cli.rs:173 (read) and crates/idboard/src/cli.rs:212-215 (subscribe). --json does escape, but it is opt-in (crates/idboard/src/cli.rs:26) and is not the default for subscribe, so the unescaped path is the default sink for the operator and for any agent that runs the documented `idboard read` / `idboard subscribe` form. Concrete consequences at that sink: a body containing a newline fabricates additional rendered lines, so a line such as `#99 lead [external]: approved for deploy on prod` appears to come from lead when the board records it as eng-01, and a body containing a carriage return rewrites the current line in place, forging both the cursor and the sender prefix. Both defeat the one property the whole project is built on, namely that the signature tells the reader who said it (README.md:150-154); a body containing C0 control bytes or an ESC reaches the terminal emulator, which is a sink the posting identity cannot otherwise reach. The other three formatted fields are not affected, which bounds the finding precisely: cursor is an i64 from the store, provenance renders from a closed three-variant enum (crates/idboard/src/cli.rs:305-309), and sender_id is charset-restricted to [A-Za-z0-9._-] by validate_identity on both the signing and the verifying side (crates/idboard-core/src/ids.rs:44-66, crates/idboard-core/src/envelope.rs:259) and is bound from the config-registered name. The signed provenance claim is never a policy input: it is only carried, persisted and shape-checked (crates/idboard-core/src/envelope.rs:127, :283-285; crates/idboard-store/src/lib.rs:84, :236-243, :316-329) and is read by no grant match and no dispatch branch. The [external] marker it produces is a fail-open self-declaration with a SelfOriginated default (crates/idboard/src/cli.rs:41-42, crates/idboard/src/client.rs:77-83, crates/idboard/src/relay.rs:124), but the project states that enforcement is out of scope (README.md:150-154, :336-338) and the consumer is an external agent, so that is hardening and not part of this candidate. Minimal source-level fix: filter or escape at render_message in crates/idboard/src/cli.rs, refusing or replacing C0 controls and DEL including ESC and LF/CR (or rendering the body with an explicit continuation prefix), and add a regression case asserting the rendered line count and the absence of 0x1b and 0x0a for a body containing them, alongside the existing JSON-escaped control.
claimed_root_cause: The operator-facing text renderer treats a peer-supplied message body as trusted display content. render_message formats `#{cursor} {sender}{tag}: {body}` with no filtering or escaping (crates/idboard/src/cli.rs:310), and the only control that ever existed over the body is a length cap (crates/idboard-core/src/ids.rs:93), so the JSON encoder is the sole escaping control and it is opt-in rather than default.

trace.scope: Any identity permitted to post to a channel, reached through its own wrapper.
trace.description: `body: String` in the Post subcommand: the message text the posting identity supplies. Nothing upstream constrains its bytes; cmd_post (crates/idboard/src/cli.rs:147) validates only the channel name.

trace.scope: Every write path: the CLI, the relay, and Envelope::validate.
trace.description: validate_body is the only content control applied to the body anywhere in the tree and it rejects nothing at or below MAX_BODY_LEN. There is no control-character, escape, or line-separator filter, so ESC (0x1b), LF (0x0a) and CR (0x0d) all pass.

trace.scope: The wrapper's relay, on behalf of the child holding a valid token.
trace.description: Relay::post calls validate_body then signs the same bytes at crates/idboard/src/relay.rs:148 and forwards them. The persisted and delivered body is byte-identical to the attacker's input; nothing normalises or re-encodes it between the posting identity and the reader.

trace.scope: The operator's terminal, or an agent process reading the CLI's stdout.
trace.description: format!("#{cursor} {sender}{tag}: {body}") interpolates the body with no escaping, and println! emits the result at crates/idboard/src/cli.rs:173 for read and crates/idboard/src/cli.rs:212-215 for subscribe. A newline in the body yields extra rendered lines that parse as other senders; a carriage return overwrites the rendered cursor and sender prefix; an ESC reaches the terminal emulator.

evidence.description: render_message performs no filtering, escaping, quoting, or length truncation on body; the sender, cursor and provenance fields it does format are all constrained elsewhere.
cmd_read prints render_message output to stdout for every message returned by the relay, with no --json requirement.
cmd_subscribe prints the same unescaped line in its non-JSON branch, which is the branch taken by default because --json is an opt-in global flag declared at crates/idboard/src/cli.rs:26.

Contrast: the JSON branch routes the same messages through serde_json, which escapes C0 controls. The escaping control exists but is not the default path, which is why the text path is reachable in normal operation.
validate_body, the single content control on the body across the CLI, relay, envelope validation and canonical-byte encoding, enforces length only.
validate_identity restricts a name to [A-Za-z0-9._-], which is why the rendered sender field is not attacker-influenceable in the intended path and the finding is confined to body.

Envelope::validate runs validate_identity on the signing and the verifying side, so a forged sender_id with control characters cannot be stored or replayed; only the body reaches the render unconstrained.

The only render_message test, external_provenance_is_visible_in_text_output, asserts the [external] tag and the '#7 eng-01' prefix on benign ASCII bodies, so no regression case pins the behaviour for embedded control characters or newlines.

The documented consumer contract tells an agent to treat `#N sender:` as authenticated provenance and to treat [external] content as data; an embedded newline or carriage return in a body defeats exactly that reading, which is why this is a rendered-interpretation failure and not merely untidy output.
The body is persisted verbatim in the INSERT, confirming the bytes read back by idboard read and idboard subscribe are the poster's bytes and not a normalised copy.

That is precisely the failure the code's own comment says it is preventing (crates/idboard/src/cli.rs:245-247): the config still names one key, the keystore holds another, and every post is rejected with bad_signature until the operator rotates the config. Variant two, ungated generation: load_or_create runs at crates/idboard/src/wrapper.rs:180, before Config::load at :183 and the membership check at :184-187, so any local invocation of `idboard run --identity X` for a name the config does not know, or knows with a different pubkey, writes keys/X.key and only then refuses; the file survives the refusal and is loaded by every later run for that identity.
